name: Setup
goal: Get to know the workbook Claude built for you.

steps.title: Meet the practice company
steps.ask: Step 1 of 2: Meet the practice company. Click the sheet named Inputs at the bottom of the screen and look at row 5. You should see 1,243.2 in E5.
steps.hint1: Sheet names are the tabs along the bottom edge of Excel.
steps.hint2: Click the tab that says Inputs.
steps.why: Kaveri Foods is a made-up packaged-foods company. Every number you need is on Inputs, so the rest of the model only links to it.

steps.title: Learn the colour code
steps.ask: Step 2 of 2: On the Inputs sheet the numbers are blue. What does blue mean in a model?
steps.after: Blue = typed inputs, black = formulas. Anyone opening the model instantly sees what they can change and what is calculated.

name: Historicals
goal: Bring the last three years onto the IS and BS sheets and prove the balance sheet balances.

steps.title: Link FY23 revenue
steps.ask: Step 1 of 13: Link FY23 revenue. Click the IS sheet. In cell C5 type =Inputs!C5 and press Enter. You should see 1,000.0 in C5.
steps.hint1: A link pulls a number from another sheet instead of retyping it.
steps.hint2: Equals sign, the sheet name, an exclamation mark, then the cell.
steps.why: Linking means if the source number changes, your model updates by itself. Retyping numbers is how models go wrong.

steps.title: Copy revenue across
steps.ask: Step 2 of 13: Copy revenue across. Click C5, then drag the small square at its bottom-right corner right to E5. You should see 1,243.2 in E5.
steps.hint1: The small square at the corner of a selected cell is the fill handle.
steps.hint2: Drag it right; Excel shifts the formula to D5 and E5 automatically.
steps.why: One formula copied across all years keeps the row consistent, which is the number one rule of clean models.

steps.title: Link the cost rows
steps.ask: Step 3 of 13: Link the cost rows. In C6 type =Inputs!C6 and drag it to E6. Do the same for rows 8, 9, 11, 13 and 15. You should see 48.5 in E15.
steps.answer: IS!C6:E6 =Inputs!C6; IS!C8:E8 =Inputs!C8; IS!C9:E9 =Inputs!C9; IS!C11:E11 =Inputs!C11; IS!C13:E13 =Inputs!C13; IS!C15:E15 =Inputs!C15
steps.yellow: IS!C6:E6, IS!C8:E8, IS!C9:E9, IS!C11:E11, IS!C13:E13, IS!C15:E15
steps.hint1: Each row on IS links to the same row number on Inputs.
steps.hint2: Row 8 is =Inputs!C8, row 9 is =Inputs!C9, and so on, each dragged to column E.
steps.why: These are the company's actual costs. You only link raw numbers; everything else you calculate.

steps.title: Calculate gross profit
steps.ask: Step 4 of 13: Calculate gross profit. In C7 type =C5-C6, press Enter, then drag it to E7. You should see 527.1 in E7.
steps.hint1: Gross profit is what is left after the cost of making the product.
steps.hint2: Revenue minus COGS.
steps.why: Gross margin shows pricing power. A food company that can pass on raw-material inflation keeps it steady.

steps.title: Calculate EBITDA
steps.ask: Step 5 of 13: Calculate EBITDA. In C10 type =C7-C8-C9 and drag it to E10. You should see 258.6 in E10.
steps.hint1: EBITDA is operating profit before depreciation, interest and tax.
steps.hint2: Gross profit minus employee costs minus other expenses.
steps.why: EBITDA is the profit the core business generates. Analysts compare it across companies because it ignores how the company is financed.

steps.title: Calculate EBIT
steps.ask: Step 6 of 13: Calculate EBIT. In C12 type =C10-C11 and drag it to E12. You should see 215.6 in E12.
steps.hint1: EBIT is EBITDA after depreciation.
steps.hint2: EBITDA minus depreciation.
steps.why: Depreciation spreads the cost of machines over their life, so EBIT is a fairer view of operating profit.

steps.title: Calculate profit before tax
steps.ask: Step 7 of 13: Calculate profit before tax. In C14 type =C12-C13 and drag it to E14. You should see 192.6 in E14.
steps.hint1: Profit before tax is EBIT after paying interest to lenders.
steps.hint2: EBIT minus interest.
steps.why: Interest is the cost of the company's debt. More debt means more interest and less left for shareholders.

steps.title: Calculate net profit
steps.ask: Step 8 of 13: Calculate net profit. In C16 type =C14-C15 and drag it to E16. You should see 144.1 in E16.
steps.hint1: Net profit (PAT) is what belongs to shareholders after tax.
steps.hint2: Profit before tax minus tax.
steps.why: PAT is the bottom line. It feeds retained earnings on the balance sheet, which is the first link between the statements.

steps.title: Link the assets
steps.ask: Step 9 of 13: Link the assets. Click the BS sheet. In C5 type =Inputs!C21 and drag it to E5, then drag C5:E5 down to row 8. You should see 465.0 in E8.
steps.hint1: Assets on Inputs start at row 21 in the same order: cash, receivables, inventory, fixed assets.
steps.hint2: Select C5:E5 and drag the fill handle down to row 8; the row numbers shift by themselves.
steps.why: Assets are what the company owns: cash, money customers owe, stock in the warehouse and factories.

steps.title: Total the assets
steps.ask: Step 10 of 13: Total the assets. In C9 type =SUM(C5:C8) and drag it to E9. You should see 985.9 in E9.
steps.hint1: Total assets adds up the four asset lines.
steps.hint2: Use SUM over rows 5 to 8.
steps.why: This total must equal what the company owes plus what shareholders own. That is the balance sheet identity.

steps.title: Link liabilities and equity
steps.ask: Step 11 of 13: Link liabilities and equity. In C11 type =Inputs!C26 and drag it to E11, then drag C11:E11 down to row 14. You should see 578.2 in E14.
steps.hint1: On Inputs, payables, debt, share capital and retained earnings are rows 26 to 29.
steps.hint2: Same trick as the assets: one link, drag right, then drag down.
steps.why: Liabilities are what the company owes; equity is what belongs to shareholders.

steps.title: Total liabilities and equity
steps.ask: Step 12 of 13: Total liabilities and equity. In C15 type =SUM(C11:C14) and drag it to E15. You should see 985.9 in E15.
steps.hint1: Add up everything in rows 11 to 14.
steps.why: If this equals total assets, the historical balance sheet is consistent.

steps.title: Build the balance check
steps.ask: Step 13 of 13: Build the balance check. In C17 type =C9-C15 and drag it to E17. You should see 0.0 in E17.
steps.hint1: The check is assets minus liabilities and equity.
steps.hint2: Total assets row minus total liabilities and equity row.
steps.why: This must be zero in every year. It is the single most important check in any 3-statement model.

name: Ratios
goal: Turn raw numbers into ratios you can reason about.

steps.title: Revenue growth
steps.ask: Step 1 of 8: Revenue growth. On the IS sheet, in D19 type =D5/C5-1 and drag it to E19. You should see 11.0% in E19.
steps.hint1: Growth compares this year with last year.
steps.hint2: This year's revenue divided by last year's, minus 1.
steps.why: Growth is the biggest driver of value. FY23 has no growth number because there is no FY22 in the data.

steps.title: Gross margin
steps.ask: Step 2 of 8: Gross margin. In C20 type =C7/C5 and drag it to E20. You should see 42.4% in E20.
steps.hint1: A margin is a profit line divided by revenue.
steps.hint2: Gross profit divided by revenue.
steps.why: A rising gross margin means the company keeps more of every rupee of sales after raw-material costs.

steps.title: EBITDA margin
steps.ask: Step 3 of 8: EBITDA margin. In C21 type =C10/C5 and drag it to E21. You should see 20.8% in E21.
steps.hint1: Same idea as gross margin, one level lower.
steps.hint2: EBITDA divided by revenue.
steps.why: EBITDA margin shows how efficiently the company runs day to day.

steps.title: Net profit margin
steps.ask: Step 4 of 8: Net profit margin. In C22 type =C16/C5 and drag it to E22. You should see 11.6% in E22.
steps.hint1: The bottom line as a share of sales.
steps.hint2: Net profit divided by revenue.
steps.why: This is how many paise of profit shareholders earn for every rupee of sales.

steps.title: Receivable days
steps.ask: Step 5 of 8: Receivable days. Click the Schedules sheet. In C5 type =Inputs!C22/IS!C5*365 and drag it to E5. You should see 45 in E5.
steps.hint1: Receivable days = how many days of sales customers still owe.
steps.hint2: Receivables divided by revenue, times 365.
steps.why: If customers take longer to pay, cash gets stuck. That is why fast-growing companies can run out of money.

steps.title: Inventory days
steps.ask: Step 6 of 8: Inventory days. In C6 type =Inputs!C23/IS!C6*365 and drag it to E6. You should see 50 in E6.
steps.hint1: Inventory is measured against the cost of goods, not revenue.
steps.hint2: Inventory divided by COGS, times 365.
steps.why: Inventory days show how long products sit in the warehouse before being sold.

steps.title: Payable days
steps.ask: Step 7 of 8: Payable days. In C7 type =Inputs!C26/IS!C6*365 and drag it to E7. You should see 60 in E7.
steps.hint1: Payables are what the company owes its suppliers.
steps.hint2: Payables divided by COGS, times 365.
steps.why: Paying suppliers later frees up cash. Kaveri pays suppliers in about 60 days but collects from customers in 45.

steps.title: Read the ratios
steps.ask: Step 8 of 8: Gross margin went from 41.5% to 42.4%. What does that most likely mean?
options: Raw materials got relatively cheaper or prices rose
The company took on more debt
steps.correct: Raw materials got relatively cheaper or prices rose
steps.after: Gross margin only involves revenue and the cost of goods, so it reflects pricing and input costs.

name: Assumptions
goal: Choose the drivers that will push the model into the future.

steps.title: Set revenue growth
steps.ask: Step 1 of 3: Set revenue growth. Click the Inputs sheet. In F32 to J32 type 12%, 11%, 10%, 9% and 8%, one per cell. You should see 8.0% in J32.
steps.hint1: Growth was 12% and 11% in the last two years. Assume it slows down gently.
steps.hint2: Type 12% in F32, 11% in G32 and so on. These are typed inputs, so they stay blue.
steps.why: Growth usually slows as a company gets bigger. Tapering it is more believable than a flat 12% forever.

steps.title: Base COGS on history
steps.ask: Step 2 of 3: Base COGS on history. In F33 type =1-AVERAGE(IS!C20:E20) and press Enter. You should see 58.0% in F33.
steps.hint1: COGS % is the opposite of gross margin.
steps.hint2: 1 minus the average gross margin of the last three years.
steps.why: Anchoring an assumption to history makes it defensible. You can always argue for changing it later.

steps.title: Keep COGS flat
steps.ask: Step 3 of 3: Keep COGS flat. In G33 type =F33 and drag it to J33. You should see 58.0% in J33.
steps.hint1: Each year uses the year before.
steps.hint2: G33 points at F33; dragging makes H33 point at G33, and so on.
steps.why: Now you can change the COGS assumption in one cell, F33, and every year follows.

name: Revenue to EBITDA
goal: Project the top half of the income statement.

steps.title: Project FY26 revenue
steps.ask: Step 1 of 7: Project FY26 revenue. Click the IS sheet. In F5 type =E5*(1+Inputs!F32) and press Enter. You should see 1,392.4 in F5.
steps.hint1: Next year's revenue is this year's revenue grown by the growth rate.
steps.hint2: Last year's revenue times one plus the growth rate on Inputs.
steps.why: Revenue drives almost every other line, so it is always projected first.

steps.title: Project all revenue
steps.ask: Step 2 of 7: Project all revenue. Drag F5 to J5. You should see 2,001.4 in J5.
steps.hint1: Use the fill handle again.
steps.hint2: Each year now grows from the year before by its own rate.
steps.why: By FY30 Kaveri's revenue is about 1.6 times today's.

steps.title: Project COGS
steps.ask: Step 3 of 7: Project COGS. In F6 type =F5*Inputs!F33 and drag it to J6. You should see 1,161.5 in J6.
steps.hint1: COGS is a percentage of revenue.
steps.hint2: Revenue times the COGS % on Inputs.
steps.why: Costs that move with sales are modelled as a percentage of sales.

steps.title: Extend gross profit
steps.ask: Step 4 of 7: Extend gross profit. Click E7 and drag it right to J7. You should see 839.9 in J7.
steps.hint1: The gross profit formula you wrote in Module 1 works for future years too.
steps.hint2: Drag the existing formula; do not retype it.
steps.why: Reusing the same formula across history and projections keeps the row consistent.

steps.title: Project employee costs
steps.ask: Step 5 of 7: Project employee costs. In F8 type =F5*Inputs!F34 and drag it to J8. You should see 194.1 in J8.
steps.hint1: Same pattern as COGS.
steps.hint2: Revenue times employee costs % on Inputs row 34.
steps.why: Salaries grow roughly in line with the business.

steps.title: Project other expenses
steps.ask: Step 6 of 7: Project other expenses. In F9 type =F5*Inputs!F35 and drag it to J9. You should see 238.2 in J9.
steps.hint1: Same pattern again.
steps.hint2: Revenue times other expenses % on Inputs row 35.
steps.why: Rent, power, freight and marketing also scale with sales.

steps.title: Extend EBITDA
steps.ask: Step 7 of 7: Extend EBITDA. Click E10 and drag it right to J10. You should see 407.6 in J10.
steps.hint1: Reuse the EBITDA formula from Module 1.
steps.hint2: Drag E10 to J10.
steps.why: You now have five years of projected operating profit.

name: Working capital
goal: Project receivables, inventory and payables, and see how they tie up cash.

steps.title: Bring in day assumptions
steps.ask: Step 1 of 8: Bring in day assumptions. Click the Schedules sheet. In F5 type =Inputs!F36 and drag it to J5, then drag F5:J5 down to row 7. You should see 60 in J7.
steps.hint1: The day assumptions live on Inputs rows 36 to 38.
steps.hint2: Link F5 to Inputs!F36, then fill right and down.
steps.why: Days are the driver; balances are calculated from them.

steps.title: Link historical balances
steps.ask: Step 2 of 8: Link historical balances. In C9 type =Inputs!C22 and drag it to E9, then drag C9:E9 down to row 10. In C11 type =Inputs!C26 and drag it to E11. You should see 117.7 in E11.
steps.hint1: Receivables and inventory are Inputs rows 22 and 23; payables is row 26.
steps.hint2: Two separate links because payables sits on a different row.
steps.why: History gives the starting point for the projection.

steps.title: Project receivables
steps.ask: Step 3 of 8: Project receivables. In F9 type =F5/365*IS!F5 and drag it to J9. You should see 246.7 in J9.
steps.hint1: Reverse the days formula you built in Module 2.
steps.hint2: Days divided by 365, times revenue.
steps.why: As revenue grows, receivables grow with it, which absorbs cash.

steps.title: Project inventory
steps.ask: Step 4 of 8: Project inventory. In F10 type =F6/365*IS!F6 and drag it to J10. You should see 159.1 in J10.
steps.hint1: Inventory days are measured on COGS.
steps.hint2: Inventory days divided by 365, times COGS.
steps.why: More sales need more stock on the shelves.

steps.title: Project payables
steps.ask: Step 5 of 8: Project payables. In F11 type =F7/365*IS!F6 and drag it to J11. You should see 190.9 in J11.
steps.hint1: Payables are also measured on COGS.
steps.hint2: Payable days divided by 365, times COGS.
steps.why: Suppliers effectively lend the company money, which offsets some of the cash tied up.

steps.title: Net working capital
steps.ask: Step 6 of 8: Net working capital. In C12 type =C9+C10-C11 and drag it to J12. You should see 214.9 in J12.
steps.hint1: Working capital is what customers and stock tie up, minus what suppliers fund.
steps.hint2: Receivables plus inventory minus payables.
steps.why: This is the cash permanently locked in day-to-day operations.

steps.title: Change in working capital
steps.ask: Step 7 of 8: Change in working capital. In D13 type =D12-C12 and drag it to J13. You should see 15.9 in J13.
steps.hint1: Compare this year's working capital with last year's.
steps.hint2: This year's NWC minus last year's.
steps.why: An increase is cash that went into the business instead of the bank. It reduces cash flow.

steps.title: Working capital and cash
steps.ask: Step 8 of 8: If customers start paying in 60 days instead of 45, what happens to cash?
steps.after: Higher receivable days means more money stuck with customers, so less cash in the bank.

name: Fixed assets
goal: Project capex, depreciation and the net block.

steps.title: Historical net block
steps.ask: Step 1 of 6: Historical net block. On the Schedules sheet, in C19 type =Inputs!C24 and drag it to E19. You should see 465.0 in E19.
steps.hint1: Net fixed assets are on Inputs row 24.
steps.hint2: =Inputs!C24, dragged to E19.
steps.why: FY25 closing net block is where the projection starts.

steps.title: Opening net block
steps.ask: Step 2 of 6: Opening net block. In F16 type =E19 and drag it to J16. You should see 465.0 in F16.
steps.hint1: This year starts where last year ended.
steps.hint2: Point at last year's closing net block in row 19.
steps.why: Every roll-forward schedule follows opening + additions − reductions = closing.

steps.title: Capex
steps.ask: Step 3 of 6: Capex. In F17 type =IS!F5*Inputs!F39 and drag it to J17. You should see 100.1 in J17.
steps.hint1: Capex is spending on new factories and machines.
steps.hint2: Revenue times capex % on Inputs row 39.
steps.why: A growing food company needs more production capacity.

steps.title: Depreciation
steps.ask: Step 4 of 6: Depreciation. In F18 type =F16*Inputs!F40 and drag it to J18. You should see 46.5 in F18.
steps.hint1: Depreciation is a percentage of the assets at the start of the year.
steps.hint2: Opening net block times depreciation % on Inputs row 40.
steps.why: Depreciation is a cost with no cash going out, which is why cash flow adds it back.

steps.title: Closing net block
steps.ask: Step 5 of 6: Closing net block. In F19 type =F16+F17-F18 and drag it to J19. You should see 628.9 in J19.
steps.hint1: Closing = what you started with, plus what you bought, minus what wore out.
steps.hint2: Opening plus capex minus depreciation.
steps.why: This closing figure will become fixed assets on the projected balance sheet.

steps.title: Depreciation into IS
steps.ask: Step 6 of 6: Depreciation into IS. Click the IS sheet. In F11 type =Schedules!F18 and drag it to J11. You should see 58.8 in J11.
steps.hint1: The income statement takes depreciation from the schedule.
steps.hint2: Link to Schedules row 18.
steps.why: This is a green link: the schedule does the work, the statement just shows the answer.

name: Debt
goal: Project debt repayments and the interest cost.

steps.title: Historical debt
steps.ask: Step 1 of 6: Historical debt. Click the Schedules sheet. In C24 type =Inputs!C27 and drag it to E24. You should see 240.0 in E24.
steps.hint1: Debt is on Inputs row 27.
steps.hint2: =Inputs!C27, dragged to E24.
steps.why: FY25 closing debt is where the projection starts.

steps.title: Opening debt
steps.ask: Step 2 of 6: Opening debt. In F22 type =E24 and drag it to J22. You should see 240.0 in F22.
steps.hint1: Same roll-forward idea as fixed assets.
steps.hint2: Opening debt = last year's closing debt.
steps.why: Every roll-forward links each year to the one before.

steps.title: Repayment
steps.ask: Step 3 of 6: Repayment. In F23 type =Inputs!F42 and drag it to J23. You should see 30.0 in J23.
steps.hint1: Kaveri repays a fixed amount each year.
steps.hint2: Link to Inputs row 42.
steps.why: Repaying debt uses cash but lowers future interest.

steps.title: Closing debt
steps.ask: Step 4 of 6: Closing debt. In F24 type =F22-F23 and drag it to J24. You should see 90.0 in J24.
steps.hint1: Opening minus repayment.
steps.why: Debt falls from 240 to 90 crore over five years.

steps.title: Interest
steps.ask: Step 5 of 6: Interest. In F25 type =AVERAGE(F22,F24)*Inputs!F41 and drag it to J25. You should see 9.4 in J25.
steps.hint1: Debt changes during the year, so use the average balance.
steps.hint2: Average of opening and closing debt, times the interest rate.
steps.why: Using the average is more accurate than using only the opening or closing balance.

steps.title: Interest into IS
steps.ask: Step 6 of 6: Interest into IS. Click the IS sheet. In F13 type =Schedules!F25 and drag it to J13. You should see 9.4 in J13.
steps.hint1: Same idea as depreciation.
steps.hint2: Link to Schedules row 25.
steps.why: Now the income statement knows the cost of the company's debt.

name: Profit
goal: Finish the projected income statement down to net profit.

steps.title: Extend EBIT
steps.ask: Step 1 of 5: Extend EBIT. Click E12 and drag it right to J12. You should see 348.8 in J12.
steps.hint1: Reuse your Module 1 formula.
steps.hint2: Drag E12 to J12.
steps.why: Depreciation is now flowing in from the schedule, so EBIT is complete.

steps.title: Extend profit before tax
steps.ask: Step 2 of 5: Extend profit before tax. Click E14 and drag it right to J14. You should see 339.4 in J14.
steps.hint1: Reuse your Module 1 formula.
steps.hint2: Drag E14 to J14.
steps.why: Interest is flowing in from the debt schedule.

steps.title: Project tax
steps.ask: Step 3 of 5: Project tax. In F15 type =F14*Inputs!F43 and drag it to J15. You should see 85.4 in J15.
steps.hint1: Tax is a percentage of profit before tax.
steps.hint2: Profit before tax times the tax rate on Inputs row 43.
steps.why: 25.17% is the rate for Indian companies under the new tax regime.

steps.title: Extend net profit
steps.ask: Step 4 of 5: Extend net profit. Click E16 and drag it right to J16. You should see 254.0 in J16.
steps.hint1: Reuse your Module 1 formula.
steps.hint2: Drag E16 to J16.
steps.why: This is projected profit for shareholders.

steps.title: Extend the ratios
steps.ask: Step 5 of 5: Extend the ratios. Select E19:E22 and drag it right to J22. You should see 12.7% in J22.
steps.hint1: Your ratio formulas work for projected years too.
steps.hint2: Select the four ratio cells in column E and drag right.
steps.why: Comparing projected margins to history is the quickest way to sanity-check a forecast.

name: Cash flow
goal: Build the cash flow statement from the IS and schedules.

steps.title: Start with net profit
steps.ask: Step 1 of 9: Start with net profit. Click the CF sheet. In F5 type =IS!F16 and drag it to J5. You should see 254.0 in J5.
steps.hint1: Cash flow starts from profit.
steps.hint2: Link to IS row 16.
steps.why: Profit is not cash. The next lines adjust profit into actual cash.

steps.title: Add back depreciation
steps.ask: Step 2 of 9: Add back depreciation. In F6 type =IS!F11 and drag it to J6. You should see 58.8 in J6.
steps.hint1: Depreciation reduced profit but no cash left the company.
steps.hint2: Link to IS row 11.
steps.why: Adding it back undoes a non-cash cost.

steps.title: Subtract working capital
steps.ask: Step 3 of 9: Subtract working capital. In F7 type =-Schedules!F13 and drag it to J7. You should see -15.9 in J7.
steps.hint1: An increase in working capital uses cash.
steps.hint2: Minus the change in NWC from Schedules row 13.
steps.why: The minus sign matters: more working capital means less cash.

steps.title: Cash from operations
steps.ask: Step 4 of 9: Cash from operations. In F8 type =SUM(F5:F7) and drag it to J8. You should see 296.8 in J8.
steps.hint1: Add the three lines above.
steps.hint2: =SUM(F5:F7).
steps.why: CFO is the cash the business actually generates from running.

steps.title: Capex and investing
steps.ask: Step 5 of 9: Capex and investing. In F10 type =-Schedules!F17 and drag it to J10. In F11 type =F10 and drag it to J11. You should see -100.1 in J11.
steps.hint1: Capex is cash going out, so it is negative.
steps.hint2: Minus capex from Schedules row 17; investing total equals capex here.
steps.why: Kaveri's only investment is in its own factories.

steps.title: Repayment and dividends
steps.ask: Step 6 of 9: Repayment and dividends. In F13 type =-Schedules!F23 and drag it to J13. In F14 type =-IS!F16*Inputs!F44 and drag it to J14. You should see -63.5 in J14.
steps.hint1: Both are cash paid out, so both are negative.
steps.hint2: Minus the repayment; minus net profit times the payout ratio.
steps.why: These are the company's payments to lenders and shareholders.

steps.title: Cash from financing
steps.ask: Step 7 of 9: Cash from financing. In F15 type =F13+F14 and drag it to J15. You should see -93.5 in J15.
steps.hint1: Add repayment and dividends.
steps.why: CFF is the net cash flowing to lenders and shareholders.

steps.title: Net change in cash
steps.ask: Step 8 of 9: Net change in cash. In F17 type =F8+F11+F15 and drag it to J17. You should see 103.2 in J17.
steps.hint1: Add the three sections.
steps.hint2: Operations plus investing plus financing.
steps.why: This is how much the cash balance grows each year.

steps.title: Opening and closing cash
steps.ask: Step 9 of 9: Opening and closing cash. In F18 type =BS!E5 and drag it to J18. In F19 type =F18+F17 and drag it to J19. You should see 322.2 in F19.
steps.hint1: Opening cash is last year's cash on the balance sheet.
steps.hint2: Opening cash plus net change gives closing cash.
steps.why: Closing cash goes back onto the balance sheet. That loop is what ties the three statements together.

name: Balance sheet
goal: Project the balance sheet and make it balance.

steps.title: Cash from the CF
steps.ask: Step 1 of 8: Cash from the CF. Click the BS sheet. In F5 type =CF!F19 and drag it to J5. You should see 657.1 in J5.
steps.hint1: Cash comes from the cash flow statement.
steps.hint2: Link to closing cash, CF row 19.
steps.why: Cash is the one balance sheet line that is never forecast directly.

steps.title: Operating assets
steps.ask: Step 2 of 8: Operating assets. In F6 type =Schedules!F9 and drag it to J6, then drag F6:J6 down to row 7. In F8 type =Schedules!F19 and drag it to J8. You should see 628.9 in J8.
steps.hint1: Receivables and inventory are Schedules rows 9 and 10; net block is row 19.
steps.hint2: Link, fill right, fill down; then a separate link for fixed assets.
steps.why: The schedules do the work; the balance sheet just collects the results.

steps.title: Total assets
steps.ask: Step 3 of 8: Total assets. Click E9 and drag it right to J9. You should see 1,691.8 in J9.
steps.hint1: Reuse the SUM from Module 1.
steps.hint2: Drag E9 to J9.
steps.why: Total assets for every projected year.

steps.title: Payables and debt
steps.ask: Step 4 of 8: Payables and debt. In F11 type =Schedules!F11 and drag it to J11. In F12 type =Schedules!F24 and drag it to J12. You should see 90.0 in J12.
steps.hint1: Both come from the Schedules sheet.
steps.hint2: Payables row 11, closing debt row 24.
steps.why: Again, the statement links; the schedule calculates.

steps.title: Share capital
steps.ask: Step 5 of 8: Share capital. In F13 type =E13 and drag it to J13. You should see 50.0 in J13.
steps.hint1: Kaveri issues no new shares.
steps.hint2: Each year equals the year before.
steps.why: Share capital only changes if the company raises or buys back equity.

steps.title: Retained earnings
steps.ask: Step 6 of 8: Retained earnings. In F14 type =E14+IS!F16+CF!F14 and drag it to J14. You should see 1,360.9 in J14.
steps.hint1: Retained earnings grow by profit and shrink by dividends.
steps.hint2: Last year's retained earnings plus net profit plus dividends (already negative on CF).
steps.why: This is the second link between the statements: profit flows into equity.

steps.title: Total and check
steps.ask: Step 7 of 8: Total and check. Select E15:E17 and drag it right to J17. You should see 0.0 in J17.
steps.hint1: Reuse your total and balance check formulas.
steps.hint2: Select E15 to E17 and drag right to column J.
steps.why: If every year in row 17 shows 0, your 3-statement model is fully linked. That is the big milestone.

steps.title: Checks sheet
steps.ask: Step 8 of 8: Checks sheet. Click the Checks sheet. In C5 type =IF(MAX(BS!C17:J17)-MIN(BS!C17:J17)<0.01,"OK","ERROR") and press Enter. You should see OK in C5.
steps.hint1: One cell that tells you if any year is out of balance.
steps.hint2: If the largest and smallest balance-check values are both zero, show OK.
steps.why: In big models you cannot eyeball every year. One check cell catches mistakes instantly.

name: DCF valuation
goal: Value Kaveri Foods from its future cash flows.

steps.title: Start from EBIT
steps.ask: Step 1 of 10: Start from EBIT. Click the DCF sheet. In F5 type =IS!F12 and drag it to J5. You should see 348.8 in J5.
steps.hint1: Free cash flow to the firm starts from operating profit.
steps.hint2: Link to IS row 12.
steps.why: We start before interest because the DCF values the whole business, for lenders and shareholders.

steps.title: Tax and NOPAT
steps.ask: Step 2 of 10: Tax and NOPAT. In F6 type =F5*Inputs!F43 and drag it to J6. In F7 type =F5-F6 and drag it to J7. You should see 261.0 in J7.
steps.hint1: Tax as if the company had no debt.
steps.hint2: EBIT times tax rate, then EBIT minus that tax.
steps.why: NOPAT is operating profit after tax, ignoring financing.

steps.title: Free cash flow
steps.ask: Step 3 of 10: Free cash flow. In F8 type =IS!F11 and drag it to J8. In F9 type =Schedules!F17 and drag it to J9. In F10 type =Schedules!F13 and drag it to J10. In F11 type =F7+F8-F9-F10 and drag it to J11. You should see 203.8 in J11.
steps.hint1: Same adjustments as the cash flow statement, but on NOPAT.
steps.hint2: NOPAT plus depreciation minus capex minus increase in working capital.
steps.why: FCFF is the cash available to everyone who funded the company.

steps.title: Cost of equity
steps.ask: Step 4 of 10: Cost of equity. In C14 type =Inputs!C47+Inputs!C48*Inputs!C49 and press Enter. You should see 12.8% in C14.
steps.hint1: CAPM: risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium.
steps.hint2: Risk-free + beta × ERP.
steps.why: Shareholders want a higher return than a government bond because shares are riskier.

steps.title: WACC
steps.ask: Step 5 of 10: WACC. In C15 type =Inputs!C50*(1-Inputs!J43). In C16 type =C14*(1-Inputs!C51)+C15*Inputs!C51. You should see 11.6% in C16.
steps.hint1: WACC blends the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt.
steps.hint2: Cost of equity × equity weight + after-tax cost of debt × debt weight.
steps.why: WACC is the discount rate: the return all investors together expect.

steps.title: Discount factors
steps.ask: Step 6 of 10: Discount factors. In F25 type =1/(1+$C$16)^F24 and drag it to J25. You should see 0.578 in J25.
steps.hint1: The $ signs lock C16 so it does not move when you drag.
steps.hint2: 1 divided by (1 + WACC) to the power of the year number in row 24.
steps.why: A rupee five years away is worth less than a rupee today.

steps.title: Present value of FCFF
steps.ask: Step 7 of 10: Present value of FCFF. In F26 type =F11*F25 and drag it to J26. You should see 117.8 in J26.
steps.hint1: Cash flow times its discount factor.
steps.why: This converts each future year's cash into today's money.

steps.title: Terminal value
steps.ask: Step 8 of 10: Terminal value. In C29 type =SUM(F26:J26). In C30 type =J11*(1+Inputs!C52)/(C16-Inputs!C52). In C31 type =C30*J25. You should see 1,877.9 in C31.
steps.hint1: The company keeps going after FY30; the terminal value captures that.
steps.hint2: FY30 FCFF grown once, divided by WACC minus growth; then discount it with the FY30 factor.
steps.why: The terminal value is usually most of the valuation, which is why the growth assumption matters so much.

steps.title: Enterprise to equity value
steps.ask: Step 9 of 10: Enterprise to equity value. In C32 type =C29+C31. In C33 type =BS!E12. In C34 type =BS!E5. In C35 type =C32-C33+C34. You should see 2,516.4 in C35.
steps.hint1: Enterprise value belongs to lenders and shareholders together.
steps.hint2: EV minus today's debt plus today's cash equals equity value.
steps.why: Debt holders get paid first; what's left belongs to shareholders.

steps.title: Value per share
steps.ask: Step 10 of 10: Value per share. In C36 type =Inputs!C53. In C37 type =C35/C36. You should see Rs 252 in C37.
steps.hint1: Divide equity value by the number of shares.
steps.hint2: Both are in crore, so the answer is in rupees per share.
steps.why: This is the number you would compare with the share price to decide if a stock is cheap or expensive.

name: Sensitivity
goal: See how much the value depends on your assumptions.

steps.title: Build the sensitivity formula
steps.ask: Step 1 of 4: Build the sensitivity formula. In D42 type =(SUMPRODUCT($F$11:$J$11,1/(1+$C42)^$F$24:$J$24)+$J$11*(1+D$41)/($C42-D$41)/(1+$C42)^5-$C$33+$C$34)/$C$36 and press Enter. You should see Rs 307 in D42.
steps.hint1: This is the whole DCF in one cell, using the WACC in column C and the growth rate in row 41.
steps.hint2: $C42 locks the column, D$41 locks the row, so it works when copied in both directions.
steps.why: Mixed references are the key Excel skill for any two-way table.

steps.title: Fill the table
steps.ask: Step 2 of 4: Fill the table. Copy D42 to every cell from D42 to H46. You should see Rs 252 in F44.
steps.hint1: Select D42, copy, then select D42:H46 and paste.
steps.hint2: The centre cell F44 should match your value per share.
steps.why: The centre of the table is your base case; everything else shows what happens if you are wrong.

steps.title: Colour it as a heatmap
steps.ask: Step 3 of 4: Colour it as a heatmap. Select D42:H46, then on the Home tab click Conditional Formatting, Color Scales, and pick the green-yellow-red one. You should see the table turn green, yellow and red.
steps.check: DCF!D42:H46 has a colour-scale conditional format
steps.hint1: Conditional Formatting is on the Home tab, in the middle of the ribbon.
steps.hint2: Color Scales, then the first option (green to red).
steps.why: Colour makes it obvious where the value is high or low without reading every number.

steps.title: Read the table
steps.ask: Step 4 of 4: Which change moves the value per share more in this table?
options: They move it by exactly the same amount
steps.after: Small changes in WACC swing the value a lot. That is why analysts always show a sensitivity table, never one number.
